title: Practice good health and grooming habits

lessons.title: Looking after your body
lessons.html:
Why personal health matters

Working with horses is hard physical work. You lift bales, push wheelbarrows, ride and walk all day. A healthy body works better and gets hurt less. Good health and grooming habits also keep you from spreading germs to co-workers and food.

Eat well

  • Eat breakfast before work. An empty stomach makes you tired and dizzy.
  • Eat a mix of foods: pap or bread for energy, beans, eggs, meat or fish for strength, and vegetables and fruit for vitamins.
  • Do not eat too much sugar, fat or salt.
  • Drink plenty of clean water, especially on hot days.

Sleep and rest

Your body needs about 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night. Yard work starts early, so go to bed early. A tired groom makes mistakes and can be kicked or fall.

Exercise and posture

Yard work is exercise, but stretch your back, legs and arms before you start. Lift with your knees, not your back.

Alcohol, smoking and drugs

Alcohol and drugs slow you down and make you careless. Never come to work drunk or high. Horses can sense this and become nervous. Smoking damages your lungs, and in a stable it can start a fire. Smoke only in the marked area, far from hay.

See the clinic

  • Go to the clinic when you are sick. Do not wait until it is serious.
  • Have regular check-ups: blood pressure, eyes, TB and HIV testing.
  • Keep your tetanus injection up to date. Tetanus germs live in soil and manure and enter through cuts. Ask the clinic about it.

Look after your mind

Stress, worry and sadness also affect health. Talk to someone you trust: a friend, family member, nurse or pastor. Ask for help early.

lessons.title: Personal hygiene and grooming
lessons.html:
Keep clean

Hygiene means keeping yourself clean to stop germs. In a stable yard you work with manure, dirt and sweat every day. Germs from manure can make you sick if they get into your mouth or a wound.

Wash your hands

Wash with soap and clean water:

  • Before you eat or prepare food
  • After using the toilet
  • After mucking out or handling manure
  • After touching a sick horse or giving medicine
  • After handling chemicals

How: wet hands, rub soap all over, between fingers and under nails, for about 20 seconds; rinse; dry on a clean towel.

Body care

  • Bath or shower every day, especially after work.
  • Use deodorant.
  • Brush your teeth twice a day.
  • Keep nails short and clean. Long nails collect dirt and break.
  • Keep hair clean and tied back when working with horses so it does not get caught.

Clothes

  • Wear clean work clothes each day. Wash overalls often.
  • Wear closed boots, never sandals, in the yard.
  • Keep work clothes separate from home clothes.
  • Wear a hat and sunscreen outside; the South African sun is strong.

Cuts and wounds

Clean small cuts with clean water and cover them with a plaster before working. Report bigger wounds to your supervisor. Watch for redness, swelling or pus, and go to the clinic if you see these.

Looking professional

On race days, shows and when owners visit, grooms represent the yard. Clean, tidy staff in neat uniform give a good picture of the business. Take pride in how you look.

Key points

  • Eat well, drink water and sleep 7 to 8 hours.
  • Never work drunk or high, and smoke only away from hay.
  • Wash hands with soap after manure, the toilet and chemicals, and before eating.
  • Bath daily, keep nails short and hair tied back.
  • Cover cuts and keep your tetanus injection up to date.
